note: Questions from the CBSE Class XII Biology board exam 2026, Q.P. code 57/1/1, published by CBSE at cbse.gov.in. Case study Q29, which depends on a diagram with an unclear part structure, is left out; other figures are described in words. Solutions are written for this portal and are not CBSE's official marking scheme.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Identify the plant in which emasculation is not required for artificial hybridisation.
questions.solution: Papaya is dioecious (unisexual flowers on separate plants), so there are no anthers to remove from the female flower.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of the immune system?
questions.solution: RBCs carry oxygen and play no role in immunity.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Select the option that shows correct statements : (i) Corpus luteum secretes progesterone. (ii) Only FSH attains a peak level in the middle of the cycle. (iii) LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle. (iv) The luteal phase of the menstrual cycle is also called the proliferative phase.
questions.solution: Both LH and FSH peak mid-cycle, and the luteal phase is the secretory phase (the follicular phase is proliferative).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Select the mismatched pair :
options: Mega diversity countries in the world – 12
Genetically different strains of rice in India – less than 1000
Robert May's estimate of global species diversity – 7 million species
questions.solution: India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Pomato was produced by fusing protoplasts of
questions.solution: Pomato is a somatic hybrid of tomato and potato.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In an ecosystem, different species occupy different levels, and a vertical distribution of species is found. This is called
questions.solution: Vertical layering of species, as of trees, shrubs and herbs in a forest, is stratification.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following sacred groves is found in Meghalaya?
questions.solution: Sacred groves are found in the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A figure shows two homologous pairs of chromosomes (carrying A/a and B/b) lining up at metaphase I in two equally probable ways. One arrangement gives gametes AB and ab; the other gives Ab and aB. Which phenomenon is expressed?
questions.solution: Random orientation of non-homologous chromosome pairs at metaphase I is the basis of independent assortment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Match Column I with Column II: a. Biolistic gun b. Chitinase c. Ti d. Ca²⁺ — i. Bacterial cell ii. Tumour inducing iii. Animal cell iv. Fungal cell v. Plant cell. Choose the option for a, b, c, d in order.
questions.solution: Gene guns are used for plant cells; chitinase breaks fungal cell walls; the Ti plasmid is tumour-inducing; Ca²⁺ makes bacterial cells competent.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The idea of use and disuse of organs for evolution of organisms was proposed by
questions.solution: Lamarck proposed that organs develop with use and degenerate with disuse, e.g. the giraffe's neck.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following statements about plasmids is incorrect?
options: Plasmids have the ability to replicate within the bacterial cell.
Their replication is controlled by chromosomal DNA.
They are autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA.
They often carry antibiotic resistance genes.
questions.solution: Plasmids replicate independently of the chromosomal DNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which connective tissue connects the ovary to the pelvic wall and uterus?
questions.solution: Each ovary is held to the pelvic wall and uterus by ligaments.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The population of melanised moths increased in industrial areas after the Industrial Revolution.
Reason (R): In the industrial environment, lichen-covered trees were replaced by soot-covered trees offering better camouflage to dark-coloured moths.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Dark moths were less visible to predatory birds on soot-covered trunks, so natural selection favoured them.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): The milk produced by the transgenic cow Rosie was a nutritionally more balanced product for human babies than natural cow milk.
Reason (R): It was human protein-enriched milk containing human alpha-lactalbumin.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Rosie's milk had 2.4 g/L of human protein (alpha-lactalbumin), which is why it was more balanced for babies.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): Flocs are masses of bacteria associated with fungal filaments in secondary treatment of sewage.
Reason (R): Flocs help in digestion of solid waste by anaerobic respiration.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: Flocs digest organic matter aerobically in the aeration tank, so R is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
Assertion (A): In a terrestrial ecosystem a much larger fraction of energy flows through the grazing food chain.
Reason (R): The grazing food chain may be connected to the detritus food chain at some levels.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation for Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution: In terrestrial ecosystems most energy flows through the detritus food chain, so A is false.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Define humoral immune response. (b) Name any two types of antibodies that give the humoral immune response in humans.
questions.solution: (a) The immune response mediated by antibodies circulating in the blood and lymph, produced by B-lymphocytes. (b) Any two of IgA, IgG, IgM, IgE, IgD.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) How does a farmer use dormancy of seed to his advantage? (ii) Differentiate between pea seed and castor seed.
questions.solution: (i) Dormant seeds can be stored for long periods and sown in the next season when conditions are favourable. (ii) Pea seed is non-albuminous (endosperm used up during development; food stored in cotyledons). Castor seed is albuminous (the endosperm persists in the mature seed).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Identify the stage of the follicle in which the primary oocyte undergoes the first meiotic division. Also mention the products of this division.
questions.solution: In the tertiary follicle, as it matures into the Graafian follicle. The primary oocyte divides unequally to form a large haploid secondary oocyte and a small first polar body.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Study the DNA sequence 5′-GAATTC-3′ / 3′-CTTAAG-5′. (a) What are such sequences called? Name the enzyme that recognises this sequence. (b) How do these enzymes function?
questions.solution: (a) Palindromic sequences; EcoRI. (b) Restriction endonucleases inspect the DNA, bind to their specific recognition sequence and cut each strand at specific points in the sugar-phosphate backbone, often leaving sticky ends.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Analyse the following two cases of sex determination : Case I: males have XO sex chromosomes and females have XX. Case II: females have two different sex chromosomes (ZW) and males have ZZ. Identify the type of heterogamety in each case, giving one example of each.
questions.solution: Case I: male heterogamety (XO type), e.g. grasshopper. Case II: female heterogamety (ZW type), e.g. birds.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Differentiate between a DNA and an RNA nucleotide. (ii) Name the two types of bonds present within a single nucleotide.
questions.solution: (i) A DNA nucleotide has deoxyribose sugar and bases A, G, C, T; an RNA nucleotide has ribose sugar and U in place of T. (ii) An N-glycosidic bond (base to sugar) and a phosphoester bond (phosphate to the 5′-OH of the sugar).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A pyramid of standing crop (biomass) is shown in which the primary producer bar (PP) is smaller than the primary consumer bar (PC) above it. (i) Identify the kind of pyramid and, with an example, explain the conditions where this kind of pyramid is possible in nature. (ii) Write any two limitations of ecological pyramids.
questions.solution: (i) An inverted pyramid of biomass, e.g. in the sea: the biomass of fish exceeds that of phytoplankton at any one time, because phytoplankton reproduce very fast. (ii) Ecological pyramids do not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels; they assume a simple food chain and ignore food webs; saprophytes are not given a place.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In an ecosystem there was loss of biodiversity due to some project in the area. (i) How will biodiversity be affected? (2 points) (ii) List two major causes of loss of biodiversity.
questions.solution: (i) Decline in plant production, lower resistance to disturbances such as drought, and greater variability in processes like productivity, water use and pest cycles. (ii) Habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasion, co-extinctions (any two).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Do all pollen grains remain viable for the same length of time? Support your answer with two suitable examples. (b) How are pollen grains stored in pollen banks?
questions.solution: (a) No. Viability depends on temperature, humidity and species. Rice and wheat pollen lose viability within about 30 minutes of release, while pollen of members of Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae stay viable for months. (b) Pollen grains are stored for years in liquid nitrogen at −196 °C (cryopreservation).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) What is pedigree analysis? Mention its importance in human genetics (2 points). (b) Analyse the following pedigree : two unaffected parents have six children — a normal son, an affected son, a normal daughter (who marries a normal man), an affected daughter and a normal son. The normal daughter and her husband have an affected son and two normal daughters. Write (i) the pattern of inheritance (ii) one example of a disease showing such a pattern.
questions.solution: (a) Analysis of the inheritance of a trait over several generations of a family using a pedigree chart. Importance: traces the origin and pattern of inheritance of a trait or disorder; helps genetic counselling and predicting the chance of a disorder in future generations. (b)(i) Autosomal recessive: unaffected parents have both affected sons and daughters, so they are carriers. (ii) Sickle-cell anaemia (also phenylketonuria, thalassaemia).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) How is the Hardy-Weinberg expression p² + 2pq + q² = 1 derived? (b) List any two factors that disturb the genetic equilibrium.
questions.solution: (a) If p and q are the frequencies of alleles A and a (p + q = 1), random mating gives genotype frequencies AA = p², Aa = 2pq and aa = q², since (p + q)² = p² + 2pq + q² = 1. (b) Gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection (any two).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Draw a neat diagram of the megasporangium (ovule) of an angiosperm and label any six parts.
questions.solution: A typical anatropous ovule attached to the placenta by the funicle. Labels: funicle, hilum, integuments (outer and inner), micropyle, nucellus, embryo sac, chalaza, and in the embryo sac: egg apparatus (egg and synergids), central cell with polar nuclei, antipodals.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (a) Mention the scientific name of the source plant and the part from which opioids are extracted. (b) How are morphine and heroin related? Mention the effect each has on the human body.
questions.solution: (a) Papaver somniferum (poppy plant); extracted from the latex. (b) Heroin (smack) is diacetylmorphine, obtained by acetylation of morphine. Morphine is a very effective sedative and painkiller, useful after surgery; heroin is a depressant that slows down body functions and is highly addictive.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A farmer grew normal corn in field A and GM corn in field B. Corn borers attacked only field A. To control them, spores of Bt were sprayed on field A. (a) Name the gene in the spores responsible for control of the pest. (b) What effect will the Bt spores have on the insect pest? (c) How have the corn plants of field B developed resistance against this pest? Explain.
questions.solution: (a) cry gene (cryIAb controls corn borer). (b) The Bt toxin exists as an inactive protoxin; in the alkaline gut of the insect it is solubilised and activated, binds to the midgut epithelial cells and creates pores, causing swelling, lysis of cells and death of the insect. (c) Field B has Bt corn: the cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis has been transferred into the corn, so the plant makes its own insecticidal protein.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A mixture of DNA fragments ranging from 100 to 1800 base pairs was loaded for agarose gel electrophoresis with the wells placed next to the positive electrode (+) and the negative electrode (−) at the far end. (a) What result will be obtained on staining with ethidium bromide? Explain with reasons. (b) The set-up was then changed so that the wells were next to the negative electrode and the positive electrode was at the far end, and a band of 100 base pairs was obtained farthest from the wells, at X. What change was made, and why did the band appear at X?
questions.solution: (a) No bands will be seen in the gel. DNA is negatively charged and moves towards the anode, which is already beside the wells, so it does not travel through the gel. (b) The electrodes were reversed (wells at the cathode). DNA moved towards the anode, and the gel sieves fragments by size: the smallest fragment (100 bp) moves fastest and farthest, so it appears at X.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A student performed some crosses in pea plants for height and plotted the number of tall and dwarf progeny as bar graphs. Cross I: 500 tall, 0 dwarf. Cross II: 375 tall, 125 dwarf. Cross III: 250 tall, 250 dwarf.

What can you infer about the genotype of the parents in crosses I and II?
questions.solution: Cross I: at least one parent is homozygous tall (TT), so all progeny are tall. Cross II: both parents are heterozygous (Tt × Tt), giving 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A student performed some crosses in pea plants for height and plotted the number of tall and dwarf progeny as bar graphs. Cross I: 500 tall, 0 dwarf. Cross II: 375 tall, 125 dwarf. Cross III: 250 tall, 250 dwarf.

Which genetic cross is represented by these crosses?
questions.solution: Monohybrid crosses (one character, height).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A student performed some crosses in pea plants for height and plotted the number of tall and dwarf progeny as bar graphs. Cross I: 500 tall, 0 dwarf. Cross II: 375 tall, 125 dwarf. Cross III: 250 tall, 250 dwarf.

Looking at the bar graph of cross III, identify the type of cross performed and its importance in genetics.
questions.solution: A 1 : 1 ratio comes from a test cross (Tt × tt). A test cross (crossing with the homozygous recessive) reveals whether a dominant-looking individual is homozygous or heterozygous.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text:
A student performed some crosses in pea plants for height and plotted the number of tall and dwarf progeny as bar graphs. Cross I: 500 tall, 0 dwarf. Cross II: 375 tall, 125 dwarf. Cross III: 250 tall, 250 dwarf.

What conclusion can you draw from the results of crosses I and II? Name the genetic principle illustrated.
questions.solution: Tallness is dominant over dwarfness, and the recessive trait reappears in the F₂ in a 3 : 1 ratio because alleles separate during gamete formation: the law of dominance and the law of segregation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Trace the events from fertilisation till implantation of the blastocyst in the human female. Also mention the site where fertilisation takes place.
questions.solution: Fertilisation occurs in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube: a sperm contacts the zona pellucida of the secondary oocyte, which completes meiosis II (forming the ovum and second polar body), and the haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote. The zygote undergoes mitotic divisions (cleavage) as it moves towards the uterus, forming 2, 4, 8 and 16-celled blastomeres; the 8–16 celled stage is the morula. The morula becomes the blastocyst, with an outer layer of trophoblast and an inner cell mass. The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium and the blastocyst becomes embedded in it: implantation, which leads to pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Some couples cannot have children though they take no precautions, and do not wish to adopt or use donors. Suggest a suitable assisted reproductive technology for each case : Case I: female normal; male has normal sperms but no connection between the epididymis and vas deferens. Case II: female has normal eggs but blocked fallopian tubes; male normal. Case III: female normal; male has a low sperm count with low motility. (ii) Copper-releasing intrauterine devices are very effective and popular contraceptives. Name any two copper-releasing IUDs. Write two reasons that make them effective contraceptives.
questions.solution: (i) Case I: sperms collected surgically from the epididymis or testis, followed by ICSI or IVF (or artificial insemination). Case II: IVF followed by embryo transfer into the uterus (IUT), since the tubes are blocked. Case III: artificial insemination (intra-uterine insemination, IUI) with concentrated semen, or ICSI. (ii) CuT, Cu7 and Multiload 375 (any two). Released Cu ions suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms; IUDs also increase phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Watson and Crick's discovery of the double helical structure of DNA was based on which two findings? Also mention the scientists associated with these findings. (ii) Write the salient features of the double helix structure of DNA (any three points).
questions.solution: (i) X-ray diffraction data of DNA by Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin; base pairing rules (Chargaff's rule: A = T and G = C) by Erwin Chargaff. (ii) Two polynucleotide chains with a sugar-phosphate backbone and bases projecting inwards; the chains are antiparallel (5′→3′ and 3′→5′); bases pair by hydrogen bonds, A=T (two) and G≡C (three); the chains coil in a right-handed helix with a pitch of 3.4 nm and about 10 bp per turn (0.34 nm between base pairs); the plane of one base pair stacks over the next, stabilising the helix.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Given below is the coding strand of the structural gene of a transcription unit : 5′-ATG ACC GTA TTT TCT GTA GTG CCC GTA CTT CAG GCA TTA-3′. (i) Write the corresponding template strand and the mRNA that will be transcribed, with polarity. (ii) If GUA of the transcribed mRNA is an intron, write the sequence of the mature (processed) mRNA (1) in a bacterium (2) in humans. (iii) How many amino acids will the resulting polypeptide have after translation in humans?
questions.solution: (i) Template: 3′-TAC TGG CAT AAA AGA CAT CAC GGG CAT GAA GTC CGT AAT-5′. mRNA: 5′-AUG ACC GUA UUU UCU GUA GUG CCC GUA CUU CAG GCA UUA-3′. (ii)(1) Bacteria do not splice, so the mRNA is the same as transcribed. (2) In humans the three GUA introns are removed: 5′-AUG ACC UUU UCU GUG CCC CUU CAG GCA UUA-3′. (iii) 10 codons remain, so 10 amino acids.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) Name the protozoan species responsible for the most serious and even fatal malaria. (ii) Name the host in which the parasite completes its sexual stages and explain the changes taking place. (iii) How does the parasite damage the human body after entering the bloodstream? (iv) Suggest two effective preventive measures to control the spread of this disease in endemic regions.
questions.solution: (i) Plasmodium falciparum. (ii) The female Anopheles mosquito: gametocytes taken up with blood develop into gametes; fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's stomach, and the sporozoites formed move to and are stored in its salivary glands. (iii) Sporozoites multiply asexually in liver cells, then attack RBCs, multiply and rupture them; release of the toxin haemozoin causes chills and high fever recurring every 3–4 days. (iv) Use mosquito nets and repellents; remove stagnant water and spray insecticides; introduce larvivorous fish such as Gambusia.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: (i) What are bio-fertilisers? (ii) Name the different types of microorganisms used as bio-fertilisers in organic farming and explain how each contributes to soil fertility. (iii) Write two advantages of using bio-fertilisers over chemical fertilisers.
questions.solution: (i) Organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil. (ii) Bacteria: symbiotic Rhizobium in legume root nodules and free-living Azotobacter and Azospirillum fix atmospheric nitrogen. Fungi: mycorrhiza (e.g. Glomus) absorbs phosphorus from soil for the plant and gives resistance to root pathogens, salinity and drought. Cyanobacteria: Anabaena, Nostoc and Oscillatoria fix nitrogen and add organic matter, especially in paddy fields. (iii) They are eco-friendly and do not pollute soil and water; they are cheap and renewable and improve long-term soil fertility.
